title: The dispersal deficit
bodyMd:
Many tropical trees produce fruits far too large for any living bird or bat to swallow whole. Botanists once treated such fruits as curiosities, but the prevailing explanation now holds that they are adapted to animals that no longer exist: the large-bodied mammals that vanished from the tropics towards the end of the Pleistocene. On this account, a tree whose seeds were once carried tens of kilometres in the gut of a browsing megaherbivore is today served only by rodents that gnaw the pulp and drop the seed beneath the parent crown.

The hypothesis is attractive and, in its broad outline, well supported. Its usual corollary is not. Researchers frequently infer that large-fruited species must therefore be in demographic decline, and some have proposed introducing surviving large mammals from other continents to restore the lost service. But that inference skips a step. A seed that travels no distance is not necessarily a seed that fails. Whether dispersal distance limits a population depends on how sharply a seedling's chance of survival falls as it germinates closer to its parent, and that relationship varies enormously among species. Where it is weak, a tree can persist indefinitely with its offspring clustered at its base. Several large-fruited species in the Atlantic forest have now been monitored for decades without any detectable decline in recruitment.

What the megafaunal hypothesis does predict, and what the field data support, is a change in spatial pattern rather than in abundance: large-fruited species are increasingly found in dense single-species clumps rather than scattered through the canopy. Clumping has consequences of its own. It concentrates a species' vulnerability to a pathogen or a windstorm, and it slows the colonisation of newly cleared ground. Those are the effects for which evidence should be sought. Treating decline as the automatic consequence of lost dispersal has directed attention away from them, and has made a costly intervention look more urgent than the data yet warrant.
accessibilityText: A three-paragraph prose passage about large-fruited tropical trees. The first paragraph describes the megafaunal dispersal hypothesis: fruits too large for any living bird or bat are explained as adaptations to large mammals that died out at the end of the Pleistocene, so that seeds once carried tens of kilometres are now merely dropped beneath the parent crown by rodents. The second paragraph accepts the hypothesis in outline but rejects the corollary that large-fruited species must be declining, and rejects the proposal to introduce large mammals from other continents; it argues that whether short dispersal harms a population depends on how sharply seedling survival falls with proximity to the parent, that this relationship varies greatly among species, and that several large-fruited Atlantic forest species have been monitored for decades with no detectable decline in recruitment. The third paragraph states what the hypothesis does predict, namely a change in spatial pattern rather than abundance, with large-fruited species increasingly found in dense single-species clumps; it notes that clumping concentrates vulnerability to a pathogen or windstorm and slows colonisation of newly cleared ground, and says that treating decline as automatic has drawn attention away from these effects and made a costly intervention look more urgent than the data warrant.
